title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 67–68
description: Advanced cause-and-effect collocations, causal reasoning, similarity, equivalence, comparison, and nuanced distinctions with accurate prepositions.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-provided textbook. Teaching targets and exercise patterns follow the source; Brazilian Portuguese translations, example sentences and explanations were written independently. Original passages, exercises, tables and artwork are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Both study pages and facing exercises for Units 67 and 68, including collocation tables, language-help notes, contrasts and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for selected short targets where confident; longer or uncertain expressions have blank IPA rather than speculative connected-speech transcriptions.

units.title: Unit 67 — Cause and effect
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 67. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish cause, produce, give and generate by typical collocations, register and positive or negative effects.
Explain sudden triggering, gradual change and emotional responses using provoke, precipitate, spark and bring about.
Use result in, stem from, grounds for, implications for and be based on with accurate complements and prepositions.
Choose natural cause-and-effect expressions for academic reports, argumentation and everyday problems.

sectionsChecked: All teaching sections, tables, language-help notes and collocation patterns
All facing-page exercises and corresponding answer-key entries

items.example: The faulty cooling system caused a costly interruption to the experiment.
items.note: Usually combines with adverse outcomes; compare the more neutral produce.

items.example: An unclear specification may cause a problem during integration.
items.note: Cause commonly collocates with problems, trouble, accidents and illnesses.

items.example: A poorly maintained signal could cause an accident at the crossing.
items.note: Cause often identifies an adverse event and its source.

items.example: The flooding caused extensive damage to the archive.
items.note: A natural collocation for an adverse physical effect; damage is normally uncountable.

items.example: The unexpected shutdown was caused by a power failure.
items.note: Passive cause + by introduces the factor responsible for a result.

items.example: Careful calibration should produce more reliable readings.
items.note: Neutral and relatively formal; frequently takes concrete results such as reports, evidence and statistics.

items.example: The panel will produce a report outlining its recommendations.
items.note: A strong formal collocation; report is usually a more natural object of produce than generate in ordinary prose.

items.example: The survey will produce statistics on household energy use.
items.note: A typical data-related object of produce; generate can also occur in technical contexts.

items.example: The audit produced evidence of repeated procedural failures.
items.note: Produce evidence means yield material supporting a conclusion; evidence is uncountable.

items.example: The revised procedure produced consistently better results.
items.note: Produce can refer to beneficial, neutral or measurable outcomes.

items.example: The unexpected award gave the researchers renewed confidence.
items.note: Less formal than cause; can convey both positive and negative effects.

items.example: Seeing the students develop their own ideas gave their tutor great pleasure.
items.note: Give someone pleasure expresses a positive emotional consequence.

items.pt: dar trabalho a alguém; causar transtornos
items.example: This ageing printer has given the office staff constant trouble.
items.note: Give trouble is a relatively conversational alternative to cause problems.

items.example: The latest figures give us a reason to reconsider our forecast.
items.note: Give someone a reason for something or to do something; choose the complement that fits.

items.example: The campaign generated substantial interest among local residents.
items.note: Formal, often involving purposeful activity, additional work or computer-created output.

items.example: The museum hopes to generate income from its new exhibition space.
items.note: Typical financial collocation; revenue and funds are also frequent objects.

items.example: The proposed restrictions generated controversy across the profession.
items.note: Generate can suggest an unintended or troublesome response.

items.example: The preliminary findings generated considerable interest in the project.
items.note: A standard collocation for attracting attention; interest here is normally uncountable.

items.example: The software can generate graphics directly from the recorded data.
items.note: Generate is especially natural for computer-created images, graphics and documents.

items.example: The unexpected changes generated extra work for the testing team.
items.note: In this collocation generate highlights an additional burden or consequence.

items.example: The minister’s remarks provoked an angry response from opposition leaders.
items.note: Especially natural for strong feelings and negative reactions.

items.example: The unexplained delay provoked anger among affected passengers.
items.note: A strong collocation for an emotional effect, generally an adverse one.

items.example: The abrupt withdrawal of funding precipitated a financial crisis.
items.note: Formal: emphasizes a rapid or dramatic event triggered by something.

items.example: A single disputed decision sparked widespread protests.
items.note: Suggests an event initiating a rapid chain of reactions; commonly negative.

items.example: The leaked memo sparked off a fierce public debate.
items.note: Phrasal version of spark in the sense of starting a reaction; spark can also stand alone.

items.example: A sustained programme of reforms brought about lasting improvements.
items.note: Often describes producing change, sometimes gradually rather than suddenly.

items.example: Improved training resulted in fewer mistakes during installation.
items.note: Cause or situation + result in + outcome; do not confuse with result from.

items.example: Many of the delays stem from incomplete documentation.
items.note: Effect + stem from + origin or underlying cause.

items.pt: ter fundamentos para; ter motivos para
items.example: The committee has grounds for questioning the reliability of the figures.
items.note: Grounds for + noun or -ing form means a defensible basis for a suspicion or action.

items.example: The appeal was rejected on the grounds that it lacked supporting evidence.
items.note: In this sense generally plural; the teaching-page pattern is have grounds for doing something.

items.example: The ruling could have serious implications for smaller universities.
items.note: Implications for refers to potential consequences, often indirect or far-reaching.

items.example: The long-term implications of the merger remain uncertain.
items.note: Often denotes consequences that must be inferred or considered.

items.example: The final recommendation was based on independently verified measurements.
items.note: A claim or argument is based on supporting information.

items.example: The unexpected variation resulted from a faulty temperature sensor.
items.note: A useful reverse pattern: effect + result from + cause. The teaching page directly teaches result in and stem from; this complementary contrast is added for clarity.

items.example: The charity event generated considerable publicity for the local shelter.
items.note: One of the source-listed objects of generate; publicity refers to public attention and coverage.

items.pt: provocar uma mudança; ocasionar uma transformação
items.example: The new policy brought about a noticeable change in hiring practices.
items.note: A key pairing reinforced by the exercises; bring about does not imply an abrupt change.

items.example: Months of preparation finally resulted in success for the team.
items.note: Result in identifies the outcome, not the originating cause.

items.pt: suscitar interesse por; despertar interesse em
items.example: The public lecture generated interest in climate modelling.
items.note: Generate interest in + topic is a conventional pattern used in the exercises.

items.example: The present difficulties stem from a series of poor planning decisions.
items.note: The stem from construction foregrounds the origins of a situation.

items.example: A sudden loss of investor confidence could precipitate a crisis.
items.note: The exercise answer key highlights precipitate and spark as especially suitable for sudden crises.

units.title: Unit 68 — Spot the difference: making comparisons
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 68. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Basic concepts · similarity, difference and comparison
learningObjectives: Express similarity or equivalence using affinity, akin to, analogy, correspond to, equate with and tantamount to.
Distinguish diverse, disparate, divergent, dissimilar, distinct, distinctive and discrete in context.
Use differentiate, diversify, diverge and distinguish with precise prepositional patterns.
Contrast comparable with comparative and select appropriate collocations such as comparative freedom and comparative silence.

sectionsChecked: All teaching sections, tables, language-help notes and collocation patterns
All facing-page exercises and corresponding answer-key entries

items.example: She felt an immediate affinity with the novelist’s portrayal of migration.
items.note: Affinity with a person or work expresses personal connection; affinity between things expresses similarity.

items.example: The researchers identified a close affinity between the two design approaches.
items.note: Use between when comparing two entities or groups.

items.example: He has always felt a strong affinity with contemporary poetry.
items.note: Use with for personal or emotional connection to someone or something.

items.example: The atmosphere at the celebration was akin to that of a family reunion.
items.note: Akin requires to; emphasizes a resemblance in character or nature.

items.example: The lecturer used an analogy to explain the feedback mechanism.
items.note: An analogy highlights a relevant similarity to clarify an unfamiliar idea.

items.example: We can draw an analogy between ecological systems and complex networks.
items.note: Collocates with between when explicitly naming both phenomena.

items.example: The survey findings do not correspond to the figures in the annual report.
items.note: Correspond to means match or agree with, not necessarily cause.

items.example: We should not equate popularity with genuine expertise.
items.note: Equate X with Y means treat them as equal in some relevant respect.

items.pt: equivalente a; praticamente o mesmo que
items.example: Failing to disclose the conflict of interest was tantamount to misleading the panel.
items.note: Usually expresses a negative equivalence; to is a preposition, so a following verb takes -ing.

items.example: These two connectors are not interchangeable despite their similar appearance.
items.note: Indicates that one thing can replace another without relevant change of function.

items.example: The replica was almost indistinguishable from the original.
items.note: Indistinguishable from means practically impossible to tell apart.

items.example: The author explores the cultural affinity between the two coastal cities.
items.note: A specific source collocation describing shared cultural features.

items.pt: diversificado; variado; composto de diferentes tipos
items.example: The panel included experts from diverse professional backgrounds.
items.note: Describes a variety of types within a collection; not the same as divergent.

items.example: The coalition brought together disparate groups with few shared priorities.
items.note: Emphasizes separation or marked difference among members of a group.

items.example: The second prototype was not entirely dissimilar to the first.
items.note: Frequently appears in not dissimilar to; it takes to, not from.

items.pt: não muito diferente de; relativamente semelhante a
items.example: Their approach is not dissimilar to the one used in earlier studies.
items.note: A restrained way of highlighting similarity through a negative construction.

items.example: The committee received divergent recommendations from the advisers.
items.note: Often used for contrasting views, opinions, interpretations or trends.

items.example: The researchers expressed widely divergent opinions on the policy’s likely impact.
items.note: A strong source collocation referring to sharply conflicting viewpoints.

items.example: A statistical association is distinct from a causal relationship.
items.note: Use distinct from; the source explicitly contrasts its preposition with to.

items.example: The instrument has a distinctive acoustic signature.
items.note: Means recognizably different or characteristic, not merely separate.

items.pt: discreto no sentido de separado; distinto e delimitado
items.example: The method divides the observations into discrete categories.
items.note: Means separate or individually defined; do not confuse with discreet (tactful).

items.example: The analysis identifies three distinct patterns of behaviour.
items.note: Points to clear separation; when stating what something differs from, use distinct from.

items.example: The tests help differentiate mechanical faults from software faults.
items.note: Often differentiate A from B or differentiate between A and B.

items.example: The classifier must differentiate between normal variation and a genuine fault.
items.note: Differentiate between A and B identifies a contrast; compare distinguish between.

items.example: The manufacturer decided to diversify its range of products.
items.note: Can mean become more varied or introduce more variety; the exercise illustrates diversify into.

items.pt: diversificar para; passar a atuar em
items.example: The company diversified into medical imaging equipment.
items.note: Diversify into specifies a new activity, sector or product category.

items.example: The two forecasts began to diverge after the initial quarter.
items.note: Physical or abstract paths can diverge; verb form associated with divergent.

items.example: Even experienced reviewers struggled to distinguish the two versions.
items.note: Distinguish X from Y or distinguish between X and Y; note the prepositions.

items.pt: comparável a; de valor, tamanho ou padrão semelhante
items.example: The overall cost is comparable to that of the earlier design.
items.note: Comparable to means reasonably similar in a relevant respect.

items.example: After a month of disruption, the department enjoyed comparative calm.
items.note: Comparative can mean relative to a less favourable situation; distinct from comparable.

items.example: Moving to university gave her comparative freedom after a tightly structured school routine.
items.note: Means freedom relative to an earlier constraint, not a direct statement that two freedoms are equal.

items.example: After the busy market closed, the square fell into comparative silence.
items.note: Means quiet relative to a previously noisy situation.

items.example: The evacuation team spent the night in comparative comfort at a local school.
items.note: Means a degree of comfort relative to less comfortable alternatives.

items.example: The two components are of comparable size but differ in weight.
items.note: Source Language help gives a comparable size as an example of being approximately alike.

items.example: Under dim lighting, the two finishes were virtually indistinguishable.
items.note: The fuller source construction is indistinguishable from something.

items.pt: grupos díspares; grupos muito diferentes entre si
items.example: It proved difficult to reach agreement among such disparate groups.
items.note: In the exercises disparate emphasises the differences separating groups.

items.example: The committee discussed the issue from divergent viewpoints.
items.note: Different points of view that lead in contrasting directions.
